An archive of data science, data analytics, data engineering, machine learning, and artificial intelligence writing from the former Towards Data Science Medium publication. # Human Priors in Object Detection. ## *What we tell the AI determines how it learns*. From all of the problems I have worked with in computer vision, the most challenging one is the object detection. This is not because the problem itself is complex to understand or bad formulated (Figure 1). But because we need to inject some strong priors about how *we think* we understand the world. That means that the stronger the priors we inject into our AI design, the more biased the AI learning will be. Beware that I am speaking about the bias in the AI learning procedure and not the bias about what the AI learns, that is a whole other topic. Ok, so what is a prior in the first place? > A prior is “a-priori” knowledge that expresses one’s beliefs about the problem at hand before tackling it. To show what I mean by injecting some strong priors, let’s consider the most widely known human prior in object detection: the *anchors*. ### Anchors as priors. If you have worked with object detection over the past few years you probably have heard about the *anchors*. results.title: Validity in Physics Research
results.content: In physics research, validity is essential to ensure that the results obtained are reliable and trustworthy. To ensure content validity, researchers should: * Clearly define the concept being measured * Identify all relevant aspects of the concept * Use multiple measurement methods to capture different aspects of the concept ### Construct Validity Construct validity refers to whether a measurement accurately measures the underlying construct. To ensure construct validity, researchers should: * Use established theories and models to guide the measurement * Validate the measurement instrument against known standards * Use multiple measurement methods to triangulate results Threats to Validity in Physics Research There are several threats to validity in physics research. * **Pilot test and validate measurement instruments**: testing and validating measurement instruments can help to ensure that they are accurate and reliable. The following flowchart illustrates the steps involved in ensuring validity in physics research: ### Using Multiple Measurement Methods Using multiple measurement methods can help to ensure that the results are accurate and reliable. To ensure the validity of mathematical expressions, researchers should: * Clearly define the variables and parameters used in the expression * Validate the expression against empirical data * Use established mathematical techniques to derive the expression Validity is a crucial aspect of physics research, and ensuring validity is essential to obtain reliable and trustworthy results. By understanding the different types of validity, threats to validity, and strategies for ensuring validity, researchers can design and conduct experiments that produce accurate and reliable results. Validity in physics research refers to the extent to which a measurement or experiment accurately measures what it is supposed to measure. Validity is important in physics research because it ensures that the results obtained are reliable and trustworthy. ### How can I ensure validity in my physics research? To ensure validity in your physics research, you can use multiple measurement methods, pilot test and validate measurement instruments, and use control groups and randomization to minimize bias. Some common threats to validity in physics research include instrumentation errors, experimenter bias, and sampling bias. To minimize instrumentation errors, you can calibrate your equipment regularly, use multiple measurement methods, and validate your measurement instruments against known standards.

results.title: Translation and Cross-Cultural Adaptation of Post-Stroke Checklist ...
results.content: This study aimed to translate the Post-stroke Checklist into Mandarin, validate its content, and cross-culturally adapt the Mandarin version of the Post-stroke Checklist (M-PSC) in line with expert review and cognitive interviewing. After translating into Mandarin, the M-PSC was modified and content validated using expert review, which resulted in a pilot version for cognitive interviewing among stroke survivors inclusive of subjects from an outpatient unit (n = 7), a rehabilitation department using traditional Chinese medicine (n = 10), and a community (n = 10). In order to use the instrument across cultures, the items need not only to be translated linguistically but also be adapted culturally to maintain equivalence between the source and target versions; this usually involves processes such as forward translation, reconciliation, back translation, expert committee review, cognitive interviewing and proofreading.9–12 The role of an expert committee is to review all the translations, make critical decisions, reach a consensus on any discrepancy, consolidate all versions of the survey questionnaire, develop a pre-final translated version in targeted language for field testing, and validate its content validity.9,11 Cognitive interviews can help researchers identify the manner in which targeted subjects understand, mentally process, and respond to the material, with a special emphasis on the unrecognized problems to minimize the bias and other classic questionnaire errors before field testing.13–15 It is viewed as an excellent method of conducting an in-depth evaluation from the patient perspective to pretest a survey questionnaire in cross-cultural adaptation.16 Therefore, the purpose of this study was three-fold: 1) to translate the PSC into Mandarin, 2) to modify the Mandarin version of the PSC (M-PSC) and validate its content by means of expert review, and 3) to culturally adapt the M-PSC according to the findings of cognitive interviews among stroke survivors. The cognitive interviewing methodology could understand how targeted subjects comprehend and generate their answers to the question, aiming to reveal problems concerning comprehension, information retrieval, judgment, and response process.13 In this study, we refined the Mandarin translation to eliminate inappropriate wording and assumptions, unintelligible terms, and double-barreled items and proposed a revised version of the M-PSC informed by the results from cognitive interviews. doi: 10.1186/s12877-019-1347-0 [DOI] [PMC free article] [PubMed] [Google Scholar%20-%20translation,%20content%20validity%20and%20cultural%20adaptation%20using%20cognitive%20interviewing%20in%20older%20mobility%20limited%20adults&author=MM%20Pedersen&author=P%20Kjaer-Sorensen&author=J%20Midtgaard&author=CJ%20Brown&author=AC%20Bodilsen&volume=19&issue=1&publication_year=2019&pages=312&pmid=31729972&doi=10.1186/s12877-019-1347-0&)].
